header: IN THE PESHAWAR HIGH COURT, ABBOTTABAD
body: Date of hearing……………….07.10.2026…………………………... Petitioner (Zafar Ali) By Mr. Muhammad Ilyas Khan, Advocate. Respondents (Mst. Arifa & others)

Respondent No.1 By Mr. Shah Faisal, Advocate. ******************* MUHAMMAD TARIQ AFRIDI, J.- Through the instant petition under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, the petitioner calls in question the judgment and order dated 24.04.2026, passed by the learned Additional District Judge-II, Battagram, whereby the appeal preferred by respondent No. 1 was allowed and the order dated 03.09.2025, passed by the learned executing Court/Judge Family Court in Execution Petition No. 20/10 of 2025, allowing the petitioner’s application for deletion of his name as attorney for the judgment-debtor, was set aside. The petitioner seeks a declaration that the impugned judgment and order is illegal, contrary to law and the facts of the case, and without jurisdiction, with the consequential relief of restoration of the executing Court’s order dated 03.09.2025.

2. Briefly stated, respondent No. 1, Mst. Arifa, instituted Family Suit No. 102/FC of 2023 against respondent No. 4 before the learned Civil Judge- II/Judge Family Court, Battagram. Respondent No. 4 contested the suit through the present petitioner as his attorney. The suit was decreed in favour of respondent No. 1 on 13.08.2024. Thereafter, she instituted execution proceedings against respondent No. 4 through the petitioner as his attorney.

3. During the execution proceedings, the petitioner moved an application seeking deletion of his name as attorney for respondent No. 4 and produced a deed dated 20.08.2025 revoking the special power of attorney executed in his favour. Respondent No. 1 contested the application by filing a reply. After hearing the parties, the learned executing Court allowed the application vide order dated 03.09.2025 and deleted the petitioner’s name as attorney for respondent No. 4 from the execution proceedings.

4. Aggrieved by the said order, respondent No. 1 preferred an appeal before the learned Additional District Judge-II, Battagram, which was allowed vide judgment and order dated 24.04.2026. Hence, the instant constitutional petition.

5. The principal question requiring determination is whether the petitioner, having represented respondent No. 4 during the suit and part of the execution proceedings, could be compelled to continue acting as his attorney after termination of his authority merely because the decree remained unsatisfied. A related question is whether the authority to conduct litigation, without any independent undertaking of suretyship, could render the petitioner personally liable for satisfaction of the decree.

6. The learned appellate Court proceeded primarily on the premise that respondent No. 1 had successfully established her claim and obtained a decree. It viewed the termination of the petitioner’s authority at that stage as an attempt to evade payment of the outstanding decretal amount, including dower and other sums.

7. Resolution of the controversy requires examination of the terms of the special power of attorney, the scope of the authority conferred upon the petitioner, and the distinction between an attorney’s representative capacity and a surety’s personal obligation. The English translation of the instrument, as reproduced, reads as follows: SPECIAL POWER OF ATTORNEY ON BEHALF OF THE DEFENDANT “I, Wajid Khan, son of Zafar Ali Khan, of the Swati tribe, originally a resident of Ajmera, Tehsil and District Battagram, and presently residing in Thailand, do hereby declare as follows: That I am residing in Thailand for employment and am the defendant in the above-titled suit. Consequently, I am unable to conduct and pursue the proceedings personally.

I, therefore, appoint Zafar Ali Khan, son of Rustam Khan, of the Swati tribe, resident of Ajmera, Tehsil and District Battagram, holder of National Identity Card No. 13202-0728779-7, as my special attorney, authorizing him to appear before the Court on my behalf and to conduct and pursue the aforesaid case.

My attorney shall be authorized to sign the vakalatnama; submit written statements, replies, applications and applications for setting aside proceedings; take all necessary procedural steps; enter into a compromise; give evidence; make statements; engage counsel; institute proceedings on my behalf; sign and verify written statements and vakalatnamas on my behalf; and file appeals before the District Court, the High Court and the Supreme Court.

He shall further be authorized to perform all acts required at any stage of the legal proceedings and to undertake all other matters relating to the aforesaid suit which I am legally entitled and competent to undertake through an attorney, including any necessary act not expressly recorded herein.

I hereby accept and ratify all acts and proceedings undertaken by my aforesaid special attorney as if performed by me personally and shall raise no objection thereto or claim any compensation for any resulting loss.”

8. A perusal of the instrument reveals that the petitioner was authorized to represent respondent No. 4 in the family suit and pursue appeals before the District Court, the High Court and the Supreme Court. The authority so conferred was confined to representation in those proceedings and did not extend to execution proceedings. In any event, the mere conferment of representative authority does not, by itself, render the attorney a judgment-debtor or a surety for satisfaction of the decree. The concluding clause further reinforces this interpretation. It is the principal who accepts and ratifies the attorney’s acts as his own. The clause does not contain any promise by the petitioner to discharge the principal’s liability or satisfy a decree passed against him.
9. To decide the controversy on the facts of the case, it is necessary to examine the distinction between a surety and a special attorney authorized to pursue the case.

10. ATTORNEY: An attorney duly appointed to pursue or defend a family suit acts on behalf of the principal, within the authority conferred by the instrument and permitted by law. Such appointment authorizes representation and the taking of procedural steps; it does not, by itself, make the attorney personally liable for dower, maintenance, dowry articles or any other relief decreed against the principal.

11. SURETY: A surety, on the other hand, undertakes an independent obligation to answer for another person’s default. Section 126 of the Contract Act, 1872 defines a contract of guarantee and the parties thereto, while section 128 provides that, unless the contract otherwise stipulates, the surety’s liability is coextensive with that of the principal debtor. The existence and terms of the guarantee therefore determine the nature and extent of the surety’s liability.

12. The same distinction is reflected in section 145 C.P.C, which contemplates enforcement against a surety only to the extent of the personal liability undertaken by him and after such notice as the Court considers sufficient. Reference to that provision illustrates the distinction between representation and suretyship; it does not proceed on an assumption that the C.P.C applies in its entirety to proceedings before a Family Court.

13. Accordingly, authority to conduct a suit, pursue an appeal or take steps towards satisfaction of a decree must be distinguished from an undertaking to satisfy that decree personally. An attorney may separately assume the obligations of a surety, but such additional liability must be established through a valid undertaking attributable to him. It cannot be inferred merely from his appointment or participation in the proceedings. Likewise, a bond securing appearance must be construed according to its terms and does not necessarily guarantee payment of the decretal amount.

14. The termination of the petitioner’s authority must also be examined in light of the provisions governing agency. Section 201 of the Contract Act, 1872 recognizes termination by the principal’s revocation of authority or the agent’s renunciation of the agency. Section 202 protects an agent’s interest in the property forming the subject-matter of the agency, while section 204 preserves acts and obligations arising from authority already exercised. Prior exercise of authority does not, by itself, make an agency irrevocable or require its indefinite continuation.

15. In the present case, the petitioner produced the revocation deed dated 20.08.2025 before the executing Court alongside an application for deletion of his name. Respondent No. 1 contested the application, which was granted, and the petitioner’s name was deleted from the execution petition. The learned appellate Court reversed that order without identifying any interest attracting section 202 of the Contract Act, 1872 or any undertaking rendering the petitioner personally liable for satisfaction of the decree. His previous participation in the proceedings and the possibility of delay in recovery were insufficient grounds to compel his continued representation.

16. The decree was passed against respondent No. 4, who remains bound to satisfy it. Deletion of the petitioner’s name as attorney neither discharges respondent No. 4 nor extinguishes or diminishes respondent No. 1’s rights under the decree. The executing Court remains competent to secure the judgment-debtor’s participation and enforce the decree through the means available under the applicable law.

17. An apprehension that recovery may become difficult or delayed cannot supply a legal basis for requiring a former attorney to continue representing the judgment-debtor. The decreeholder’s entitlement is to lawful enforcement of the decree against the person liable thereunder; it does not extend to insisting upon continued representation through a particular attorney after termination of his authority.

18. By treating respondent No. 1’s right to recovery as a right to insist upon the petitioner’s continued representation, without identifying any subsisting authority or independent obligation justifying that course, the learned appellate Court committed a material error of law warranting interference in constitutional jurisdiction.

19. Consequently, the writ petition is allowed. The judgment and order dated 24.04.2026, passed by the learned Additional District Judge-II, Battagram, is set aside, and the order dated 03.09.2025, passed by the learned executing Court/Judge Family Court in Execution Petition No.20/10 of 2025, is restored. The petitioner’s name shall stand deleted as attorney for respondent No. 4.

20. The executing Court shall proceed with execution against respondent No. 4 in accordance with law, after ensuring such notice as may be required. The decree dated 13.08.2024 and respondent No. 1’s rights to its enforcement shall remain unaffected. There shall be no order as to costs.
